rule: Stop the scroll in the first 1 to 2 seconds with motion, and state the value, the offer, the price or the result within 3 seconds. The first frame must make sense with no sound.
short: Motion in the first frame; the value, offer, price or result within 3 s; it must read with no sound.
why: Top ads keep 50 to 60% of viewers at 3 s (article sources); most people watch muted. 6 of 10 Rwandan seller ads on TikTok put the price, the offer or the number up in the first 3 s; the most-liked Rwandan phone-shop clip (@rujamaphones, 5,200 likes) is a seller in the shop holding three boxed phones with spec cards.

rule: Put the price (or the offer in a few words) in the first frame, large, in the top third of the screen, not in a bottom caption.
short: The price (or the offer) in the first frame, large, top third.
why: Four of the five cited ads put the price or the offer in the first frame (48,000RWF, PROMO FOR 5K, Offer today at Kes 2,100); one has run 522 days (Fitae), the others are 5 to 26 days old. Among the 20 long runners only 7 show any price, so this is what short-lived product ads do, not what every long runner does.

rule: Put a large first caption of about 5 words on screen at 0.0 s, in the upper-middle.
short: A first caption of about 5 words at 0.0 s, upper-middle.
why: 63% of top ads use text in the first frame (source claim); the platform UI covers the bottom.

rule: Write the hook in plain person-style words: a question, a POV line or 'I found ...', not a brand slogan.
short: Hook in plain person words (a question, 'POV: ...', 'I found ...'), not a slogan.
why: The repeated hooks were 'Urgent order?', 'POV: You just found ...', 'Nobody warns you ...'.

rule: Show the product doing its job (or the result) before any persuasion: in the first 3 s, and at least 3 uses, angles or colours within 10 s.
short: Show it working (or the result) in the first 3 s, and 3 uses, angles or colours within 10 s.
why: The blender doing juice, mango and grains answers 'what can I use it for'; a steamer demo with no text got 235.8K likes.

rule: In a before/after, show the result first ('After' or 'Wait for it...'), then the before, then the process, then the offer.
why: Several of the before/after clips open on the after frame; the reward up front keeps people watching.

rule: Default 15 to 25 s for products and offers; 6 to 9 s for a one-idea clip; a 3 to 6 s still loop as the cheap always-on version for gifts, flowers, shoes and skincare; 45 to 90 s for services with a named expert or owner talking (clinic, school, property, travel), with sentence-by-sentence captions and a fixed contact block.
short: 15 to 25 s for products and offers; a 3 to 6 s loop for gifts and fashion; 45 to 90 s for a service with a talking expert.
why: Rwandan long runners (60+ days live) have a median of 48 s and two thirds run over 35 s, mostly services with a talking person; the exceptions are 3 to 6 s loops (a bouquet, skincare, shoes) that cost almost nothing to keep running.

rule: Change the shot or the text every 2 to 4 seconds (about 3 to 5 changes per 10 s); kinetic text and colour-beat ads can go to 8 to 10.
short: A new shot or text change every 2 to 4 s.
why: Product, price and phone clips ran 3 to 5 cuts per 10 s; the fastest motion-graphics ads change colour about once a second.

rule: One product, one idea, one offer per video.
why: One product, one price, one number (Best Burgers) runs; mixed messages lose muted viewers.

rule: Put proof in the middle: a real customer reacting, the product working, a real shop full of stock, a real number from the owner.
why: Real customers eating or trying the product drove local engagement more than polish.

rule: For a 3D look, float the product in the middle with 4 to 8 ingredients, splashes or bubbles around it; one colour or a simple set behind, shallow depth of field.
why: The best 3D ads suspend the product with what it is made of around it (serum in bubbles, bread slices, milk-tea splashes).

rule: Use a three-beat reveal: 0-2 s a macro detail with a rim light; then the full product in a themed set with a slow orbit or push-in; the last 2-3 s the brand or price card on a clean background.
why: A 17 s and a 24 s premium example both follow it and end on the brand name in wide-spaced capitals.

rule: Make giant text part of the scene: the product name or the flavour or colour word, huge, behind or beside the product, cut by the frame edge, swapping colour per beat.
why: BREAD, BLURE and FRUIT / MILKTEA all do it; it reads at a glance and looks designed.

rule: Animate text on the beat: one phrase of 2 to 4 words per beat with one highlighted key word, pop-in with overshoot or a slide with motion blur, each held 0.5 to 1.5 s. A locked camera for text cards, a moving camera for products.
short: One phrase of 2 to 4 words per beat, one key word highlighted, each held 0.5 to 1.5 s.
why: Every kinetic typography example uses one phrase at a time with one key word in colour.

rule: Keep the phone or WhatsApp number on screen from second 0 to the last frame, in a fixed bar (top, or a lower-middle band above the app's UI), big digits grouped the way people read them.
short: The phone/WhatsApp number on screen from 0 s to the last frame, in a fixed bar above the app's UI, digits grouped.
why: A permanent phone bar is the commonest pattern in Rwandan ads (Eguriro, EHA 250, Kex Group, homeofhybrid, Elohome); only brands with budgets skip the number. On Instagram, 10 of 34 Kigali business reels keep the number on screen for all or most of the clip (12 show it at some point); those 10 had median 73.4K plays against 36.0K for the other 24, and 46 against 6.5 plays per follower (a direction, not proof), among them La Paix Technology (161K plays on 751 followers) and Home of Hybrid (110K on 59).

rule: Show the price as a solid box that stays up, or as a label riding on each product shot; a price list is one card that stays long enough to read.
short: The price in a solid box that stays up, or a label riding on each product.
why: Price cards are solid boxes in the Rwandan sample; East African sellers label every product (150/=, KSH 35). None of the 34 Kigali Instagram reels shows the price on screen (an amount appears in 3 captions), so a price badge is a free edge over the competition; Naivas's orange price badges show how. Under 20 Kigali Instagram reels, 72 of 177 comments (41%) ask the price (61 to 63% under shoes, skincare and hair reels, 50% under phones), and viewers complain 'Mujye muvuga n'ibiciro' (say the prices too).

rule: Place the price, the claim and the call to action in the top third or the middle; never in the bottom 15%, which the app's username and caption cover.
short: Price, claim and call to action in the top third or middle, never the bottom 15% (the app covers it).
why: On 9:16 the platform UI covers the bottom; Facebook winners put price and number in the top third.

rule: Never more than 2 lines of text at once: short sticker words that change with the beat for the story, and a fixed strip for the price and the phone.
short: At most 2 lines of text at once: short beat words plus a fixed price/phone strip.
why: homeofhybrid spells a sentence with one word sticker per beat over a permanent phone bar (468 days running).

rule: Animate spec words in as they are said: one phrase at a time, white bold with an outline or in white rounded boxes.
why: Phone shops in Kigali do exactly this ('One SIM + eSIM', 'Accessories included').

rule: Always burn in captions, even when someone speaks: sentence by sentence in a box, or word by word.
short: Burn in captions for every spoken line (most people watch muted).
why: Most viewers watch muted; the clinic's boxed captions match the speech so the 60 s talk still works.

rule: The Seedance clip has no text: open on motion, keep the top third and a lower-middle band visually calm for the price strip and the phone bar BuPulse adds on top, and end on a clean hero shot with space above it.
short: No text in the clip: open on motion, keep the top third and a lower-middle band calm for BuPulse's price strip and phone bar, end on a clean hero shot with space above.
why: Seedance garbles letters; the winning ads still need the price and the number on screen from second 0, so they are added as an overlay.

rule: End with ONE named way to order, in the middle of the frame: 'WhatsApp {phone}', 'Call {phone}', 'Order on {app}', 'Find us at {landmark}' or 'DM now before stock ends' (only if stock is really limited).
short: End with ONE named way to order in the middle of the frame (WhatsApp, call, the app, the landmark).
why: Of 51 Rwandan Facebook video ads, 22 use the WhatsApp button, 13 send to Instagram and 4 to 'Call now'; 35 put the number in the caption. Food, event and brand reels on Instagram drew 97 to 100% praise and no questions at all: no way to buy was shown.

rule: Put the offer and the price as a large overlay and repeat them in the call to action.
why: The viewer who decides at the end sees the reason and the route together.

rule: Add one trust line when the owner gives it: 'Pay after delivery', 'Free delivery in Kigali', 'Free delivery from 50k', '30 days return', a real address.
short: One trust line only if the owner gave it: pay after delivery, free delivery, returns, the address.
why: 'Free delivery' plus 'Pay after delivery' is the loudest pattern of the cash-on-delivery sellers that ran 7 to 24 months.

rule: Show where: the area and a landmark the way Kigali people give directions (Gishushu, Kicukiro Sonatube, City Tower, Chic building ground floor shop DE011), with the opening hours, in the last 3 seconds, and the area again in the caption's first line.
short: Show where: area and landmark (and hours) in the last 3 s, and the area in the caption's first line.
why: Of 51 Rwandan Facebook ads, the addresses are landmarks, not streets ('Next to DELIGHT HOTEL', 'opposite IPRC traffic lights', 'same building as boho, door 8'): this is how Kigali people find places. On TikTok, 10% of 450 comments ask where ('Mukorerahe?', 'Kigali is big, say the area'), most on clips with no address in the video.

rule: Run a recurring offer as a weekly series with the same badge and layout (Tuesday pizza, Wednesday burger, lunch Monday to Friday).
why: Kigali restaurants already do it; a series builds the habit and is cheap to repeat.

rule: A percentage off always comes with the real price ('37.5% off: 5K'); a was/now anchor only when the owner gives both prices.
why: Pairing the percentage with a concrete price makes the saving feel real.

rule: If there is a voice-over, it starts by 0.5 s; music stays under the voice; one sound effect on each reveal.
why: Voice-over by 0.5 s and a first cut by 1.5 s is the pacing of top ads (secondary sources).

rule: The voice cannot speak Kinyarwanda or Swahili: for those businesses the on-screen text and the caption stay in the content language and the voice speaks English (Claude engine); the Seedance clip has music and ambient sound only.
short: The voice cannot speak Kinyarwanda or Swahili: say lines in English, on-screen text and caption in the content language (Seedance: music and ambience only).
why: Owner rule, 17 October 2026 (voice-language.ts).

rule: Match the audience, per ad: English with Kinyarwanda touches for services, hotels, clinics, schools, tech and beauty; Kinyarwanda for plots, household goods, cheap goods and baby products; a mix for food, phones and fashion; Swahili in Tanzania, English in Kenya and Uganda. The call to action can be bilingual next to the number ('Karibu', 'waduhamagara cg ukatwandikira'). Write numbers and money the local way (38,000 RWF, 48K, 400K / month).
short: Rwanda: English with Kinyarwanda touches for services; Kinyarwanda for plots, household and baby goods; a mix for food, phones and fashion; money the local way (38,000 RWF, 48K).
why: 17 of 20 Rwandan long runners (services, considered purchases) are in English; the short-lived Kinyarwanda ads are plots and cheap goods; Derma alternates English and Kinyarwanda by video with the same address block.

rule: When a host appears, let them open with a Kinyarwanda greeting on screen ('Muraho', 'Murakaza neza').
why: A local welcome plus a real shop floor builds trust (Abby Home).

rule: Show a real place behind the product (the shop shelf, the counter, the table, the compound) and a real person or real hands; not a blank studio.
short: A real place behind the product (shelf, counter, table, compound) and real people or hands; no blank studio.
why: Real shops with real people got more local engagement than premium AI clips; real cars in a real compound ran 15 months.

rule: If there is no presenter, use hands on the product (lifting, unwrapping, turning, pouring).
why: Hands unwrapping a burger (Best Burgers), holding phones with the number on screen, unboxing and showing a ring carry the cited local and East African clips when no one presents.

rule: Default to a native, phone-made look for local sellers; keep the premium 3D and cinematic looks for premium products, and even then keep the price and the number in the motion.
short: A native phone-made look for local sellers; premium 3D only for premium products, still with price and number.
why: The two AI creators' cinematic product clips had 3.4K and 4.3K likes; phone-made clips of real Kigali shops with the number on screen reached far on Instagram (La Paix Technology 161K plays on 751 followers, Home of Hybrid 110K on 59). The accounts are unlike, so this is a direction, not proof. In TikTok round 4, real Rwandan shop clips with the price and the number on screen drew a median 1,213 likes and 42 comments, against 309 likes and 5 comments for AI studios' sales demos (7 against 14 clips, rough medians).

rule: Write the post caption with: the product and the price or offer in the first 60 characters, the phone or WhatsApp number labelled 'Call/WhatsApp:' (a second number is fine), the area and a landmark on a 📍 line, the delivery line only when the owner delivers, and the platform's hashtags.
short: Caption: product and price in the first 60 characters; 'Call/WhatsApp: {phone}'; 📍 area and landmark; delivery only if true.
why: In 111 Rwandan captions the phone is there in 63%, a place in 77%, a price in 58%, a call to action in 71%; the strongest (property, restaurants, phone shops) carry all four. The video is the proof, the caption is the contract. On Instagram, 17 of 34 Kigali reels put the phone or a DM/WhatsApp line in the caption (13 with a number), with landmarks such as 'TCB Building room 25AB', delivery and payment; none shows the price on the video itself.

rule: Hashtags by platform: Facebook 0 to 3 (the city plus the sector, e.g. #Kigali #KigaliFood); TikTok and Instagram 4 to 6 (#Kigali or #KigaliTikTok, #RwandaBusiness, one sector tag, one brand tag, #fyp if wanted); Shorts #shorts plus the city. Never 10 or more; #MadeInRwanda only for goods made in Rwanda.
short: Hashtags: Facebook 0 to 3, TikTok and Instagram 4 to 6, Shorts 0 to 3; the city first; never 10 or more.
why: Facebook ad captions have a median of 1 hashtag (49% none); TikTok captions a median of 5; #MadeInRwanda appeared in none of 125 captions.

rule: Build a campaign, not one clip: 8 to 15 variants of one format (one topic, product or dish per video), each with its own hook line, all sharing the same address, number and button; keep the best running and add to it instead of replacing it.
short: Versions: one format, many variants (own hook each), same address, number and button.
why: The longest-running Rwandan advertisers keep one format and many variants live: Derma Skin Clinic 17 ads seen since March, Elohome 8, Magic Chef 7, Piramie 6 in 11 days.

rule: Make a series, not one-offs ('New stock Sunday', 'Shop finds Ep 2', one dish per video), with the same layout each time.
why: Numbered series and one-dish-per-video advertisers keep viewers coming back.

rule: When the owner accepts MoMo, say it ('Pay with MoMo') in the end card and the caption.
why: MoMo is rare in Rwandan ads: none of the first 51 Rwandan Facebook video ads or the 111 Rwandan captions mentions MoMo, M-Pesa or Airtel Money; the Sofar Kigali ticket ad is the exception ('MoMo: 0788617015'). Saying it is an easy way to stand out.

rule: Make the 9:16 clip so it works on TikTok and as a Facebook ad (price and number in the picture, not only in the caption); change the caption per platform.
why: Facebook advertisers reuse their TikTok clips: TikTok watermarks show in two of the cited Facebook ads (Eguriro, SPOT SALON), and the same reuse shows on a YouTube Short.

rule: One idea and one price (or one offer) on screen from frame 0 and pinned there: a price pill at the top or a bar in the lower third, the same on every frame.
short: One price or offer pinned from frame 0 (a top pill or a lower-third bar), the same on every frame.
why: The most repeated Rwandan ads all do it: '20 Mbps | 20K / month' (Piramie, 6 variants in 11 days), '48,000RWF', 'Price: 500k', '350M RWF', 'Price: 16M'.

rule: Open on the best visual in frame 0 (a macro of the product, the splash, the reveal), never on a logo card; the logo comes at the end.
short: Open on the best visual in frame 0, never a logo card.
why: On Shorts the macro and splash openers got 9K to 32K likes; the motion-graphics service reels that open on a logo card got a few hundred.

rule: On YouTube Shorts keep the top 10% clear for YouTube's auto-captions and the bottom 25% for the title, channel and Subscribe button; put prices and the number at 40 to 60% height.
short: Shorts: top 10% clear (auto-captions), bottom 25% clear (title, Subscribe); price and number at 40 to 60% height.
why: YouTube draws auto-captions at the top and the channel, title and Subscribe button over the bottom third (visible in 4 frames); one Short that doubled the captions looks cluttered.

rule: Write the Short's title with the promise, the number or the product name in the first 40 characters, the shop name and city for search, the phone number for a local shop, and #shorts with the city at the end.
short: Title: the promise, number or product in the first 40 characters; shop and city; the number for a local shop; #shorts and the city at the end.
why: Shorts are found by search: the titles that carry a promise or number ('5 reasons to invest in Rwanda', 'DAY 8') are the hooks; local shop Shorts put the number in the title.

rule: End a Short with a one-line pointer in the middle of the frame (YouTube's title, captions, channel and Subscribe button cover the top and the bottom): the number, 'WhatsApp {phone}', a QR code, a 'CONTACT US' end card or the shop name to search.
short: End on one pointer in the middle (the top and bottom are covered): the number, WhatsApp, a QR code, a CONTACT US card or the name to search.
why: Shorts have no ad button; the best-liked service reel ends on a QR code and 'Contact us today' (27K likes).

rule: Never rely on words inside a generated image or clip (a label, a price, a menu): draw them as text on top.
short: Labels, prices and menus are drawn as text on top, never left to a generated image.
why: AI-made Shorts show garbled labels and menus ('WAT% CONET OL', 'SHISH KKIAA').

rule: In a Kinyarwanda caption, use the call to action Rwandan sellers write: 'Duhamagare cyangwa utwandikire kuri WhatsApp: {phone}', 'twandikire cg uduhamagare', and 'kuri {price} gusa' before a price; never a translation of 'click the link'. Keep product names, models and RWF as they are.
short: Kinyarwanda CTA: 'Duhamagare / Twandikire kuri WhatsApp: {phone}', 'kuri {price} gusa'; product names and RWF unchanged.
why: The corpus's Kinyarwanda captions use Duhamagare (9), Twandikire (8) and 'kuri' before a price (16).

rule: Lay a caption out the way its sector does: one fact per line with an icon (🏡 💰 🛏️ 📍 ✅ 📞) for property, clinic and school; a single line for a plain product. 150 to 350 characters for shops and food, 250 to 500 for property and services, rarely over 600 (schools, clinics, services and property may run to 1,000); TikTok one or two lines then hashtags.
short: Layout: icon checklist for property, clinic, school; one line for a plain product; shops 150 to 350 characters, property 250 to 500, rarely over 600 (schools, clinics, property: up to 1,000).
why: Facebook ad captions: median 316 characters and 7 lines; real estate 305 characters in 9 lines; TikTok one line of 184 characters. 19 of 125 real captions run past 600 characters, all school, clinic, service or property captions.

rule: For services and considered purchases (clinic, school, travel, furniture, internet, property), the offer may be 'book a consultation', 'visit us' or 'get a free quote' instead of a price; ask for a price only for goods, and show it whenever there is a real one ('from 20,000 RWF a night', '40,000 RWF + free delivery').
short: Services: the offer can be a consultation, a visit or a free quote; goods show their price.
why: Only 7 of the 20 long-running Rwandan ads show a price or an offer; they are mostly services and considered purchases where the next step is a visit or a call.

rule: Put the way to order in two places: the platform's button (WhatsApp, Call now or Messages) and the caption (the number and the landmark address); never rely on the button alone.
short: The route twice: the button and the caption (number and landmark); never the button alone.
why: 11 of 20 long runners put the number in the caption as well as the button; the seven that rely on the button alone are apps, tours and tax services, not shops.

rule: On Instagram, a before/after uses the same framing for both halves, one lowercase word each ('before...', 'after'), a hard cut, and holds each half 2 to 3 s.
short: Instagram before/after: same framing, 'before...' then 'after', a hard cut, 2 to 3 s each.
why: Two images and two words got 255K likes and a room remodel 1.4M; the before comes first on Instagram.

rule: One caption style per video: highlighter boxes, word-by-word kinetic captions (1 to 3 words), or one big statement held; one font family, white plus at most two colours, one key word per line emphasised by size or colour; 3 to 7 words a line, at most 3 lines.
short: One text style per video (boxes, word-by-word, or one statement), white plus up to two colours, one key word stressed.
why: Every repeating style on Instagram (the fitness coach's yellow boxes, the agent's word-by-word captions, the small-business statement) keeps one style for the whole reel.

rule: Make short product and gift reels loop: end on a frame close to the first, so the replay is seamless, and keep them under 15 s when possible. A service process or a shop walk-through may run 15 to 30 s in one take (one-take-process).
short: Product and gift reels: end close to the first frame so it loops; under 15 s when possible.
why: Many 6 to 11 s reels end on their first frame, so the loop is invisible (the 118K and 687K small-business hits are 6.7 s and 7.6 s).

rule: On Instagram, a comment keyword ('Comment PRICE', 'Comment OFFER') may sit beside the number and the place in the caption, never instead of them.
short: Instagram: a comment keyword ('Comment PRICE') beside the number, never instead of it.
why: The four reels with a comment keyword drew 170 to 182K comments, three far above their peers; the shops that sell still give a number.

rule: When the footage, the presenter or the product images are generated, say so: keep the platform's 'AI-generated' label on, and never present a generated person as a real customer.
short: Generated footage keeps the 'AI-generated' label; a generated person is never a real customer.
why: Instagram labels AI videos itself ('AI content', 'AI-generated profile' on 6 of 58 rows); hiding it costs trust and breaks platform rules.

rule: For clinics, pharmacies and schools, open with trust and the owner's own numbers (since 1969, 6 branches, the insurers accepted, 17 schools, the intake date), not a price; prices belong on shelf tags or in the caption. Product sectors (fashion, salons, car hire) lead with the price.
short: Clinics and schools open with trust and numbers (since, branches, insurers); products open with the price.
why: The Kigali pharmacies, clinics and schools that hold attention lead with 'since 1969', '6 Branches across Kigali', 'We work with EDENCARE, SONARWA, and RSSB', '17 SCHOOLS'; the fashion, salon and car-hire clips put '8k', '28k only' and '50,000 RWF per day' in the first frame.

rule: End on a clean contact card in the last 2 to 3 seconds: 'CONTACT US' (or the route) and the number large on a plain background, nothing else.
short: Last 2 to 3 s: a clean 'CONTACT US' card with the number large.
why: The clinics end on a clean 'CONTACT US +250 ...' card, which reads better than a number left only in the caption; the best-liked Shorts service reel ends on a QR and 'Contact us today'.

rule: Never let a clip depend on its audio: build the message in text and picture, put the sound under it, and burn in captions for every spoken line.
short: Never depend on audio: the message is in text and picture; sound goes under it.
why: Of 30 clips checked for sound, 12 carry the message in on-screen text, 11 in the picture alone and 7 by a speaker, all 7 with burned-in subtitles; most people watch muted.

rule: Choose the music kind, not a track, from BuPulse's royalty-free library: afro (mid-tempo Afrobeats or amapiano) for salons, fashion, travel and unboxing; energetic for street wear; calm for clinics, pharmacies and schools. Never a trending or copyrighted song.
short: Music: afro for salons, fashion, travel, unboxing; energetic for street wear; calm for clinics and schools; never a trending track.
why: The named tracks on Kigali salon, fashion, travel and unboxing clips were Afrobeats and East African (Victony, Ayra Starr, Maurice Kirya), street wear used hip-hop, and the clinics and schools used calm sound or a speaker.

rule: Use a voice when a person or a story carries the clip (a presenter, a student, a doctor, a vlogger), always with burned-in subtitles; in shop, menu and price clips the text carries the message, and any voice keeps to one short line per beat that matches the on-screen text.
short: Voice for a person or a story, always subtitled; in price clips the text leads and the voice matches it line by line.
why: The 7 voice-led clips are a presenter, a student, a doctor or a vlogger, all subtitled; shop, phone and menu ads carry the message in text. Under a Kigali shop reel a viewer asked 'Jyuvuga cyane twumve' (speak up so we can hear): keep the voice clear and captioned.

rule: Land each text change (every 2 to 4 s) and the product reveal on a beat of the music, with one sound hit on the reveal.
short: Text changes and the reveal land on the beat, a sound hit on the reveal.
why: In text-led clips the phrase or the price changes every 2 to 4 s; 3D and kinetic clips put a hit on the reveal.

rule: Show the full price on screen in a label that stays up, with its condition in the same label ('28k with extension', '133k for 3 nights', 'from 7.5K RWF'); never leave the price for the comments or a DM.
short: The full price on screen with its condition in the same label ('28k with extension', '133k for 3 nights').
why: Price questions are 21% of 450 comments on 30 clips, and 69 of the 94 are on clips with no price on screen (15 of 20 comments on one Kigali hair-extension clip ask 'angahe'); a fashion clip that showed '8k' and answered '18k' in the comments was called a lie ('Urabeshya').

rule: Label the number with what it is for ('WhatsApp 0788 …', 'Call 0788 …'), large and held to the end; for a seller who delivers, add one line ('Delivery in Kigali · Pay on delivery'), only if true.
short: Label the number ('WhatsApp …', 'Call …'); add the delivery line when the owner delivers.
why: Viewers ask for the number (4% of comments) even when it is on screen or in the caption ('is that number WhatsApp?'); a bedding clip drew delivery questions ('payment after delivery?', 'do you deliver to the provinces?'). On Instagram, 'Nimero', 'Number plz' and 'Contact?' come up even under reels that give the number in the caption.

rule: Pre-answer the standard questions in the caption's first line (what shows before 'more'): the price, the area, what is included, sizes or colours, delivery and how to order; and give the seller a first comment to post ('Price: … Location: … WhatsApp: …').
short: Caption first line answers price, area, what is included, sizes, delivery, how to order; plus a ready first comment.
why: About three of four viewer questions get no visible answer (44 of 177 had a seller reply beside them); the replies that worked were specific (a price, an address, one clear route). On Instagram, sellers answered 46 of 86 questions and 19 of 38 price replies only said 'DM'; one reel's 227K plays left 14 price questions with one reply. A first comment for the seller to pin (price, place, delivery, WhatsApp) answers them once.

rule: A clinic or pharmacy that takes insurance names the insurers accepted on screen for at least 2 to 3 seconds and in the caption (only the owner's list).
short: Clinics: the insurers accepted on screen for 2 to 3 s and in the caption.
why: A Kigali clinic clip drew 11 insurer questions out of 15 comments (RSSB, MMI, Old Mutual, Mituelle) although a poster listed insurers for a few seconds.

rule: Prove it is real: keep the real shop, the real stock and a real person or real hands in frame; AI-assisted visuals keep the real product photo recognisable and never invent a place, a campus or a shop.
short: Real shop, stock and hands in frame; AI visuals keep the real product photo and never invent a place.
why: 'ni AI' and 'is this AI generated?' appeared on a Chinese campus posted as a Rwandan school and on a Kigali fashion clip; real shop, person and stock answer most trust doubts. In TikTok round 4, real Rwandan shop clips with the price and the number on screen drew a median 1,213 likes and 42 comments, against 309 likes and 5 comments for AI studios' sales demos (7 against 14 clips, rough medians).

rule: For a treatment, a repair or a service, film or design one satisfying process in one continuous take (1 to 4 cuts per 10 s, 15 to 30 s): the claim or 'Day 7' on screen at 0 s, the process once, then the booking line (area and number) in a strip that stays.
short: Services: one process in one take, 15 to 30 s, 1 to 4 cuts per 10 s; the booking line (area and number) stays on screen.
why: Kigali's furthest-reaching service reels are single takes: Elysian Spa's scrub (286K plays on 4.1K followers), the microlocs hair flip (193K and 171K on 4.6K), a NeoDerma facial (32K). Kigali business reels run a median 27 s against 13 s for the global sample, with 1 to 4 cuts per 10 s. The sample is each account's top reels, so it shows what wins, not the average.

rule: A bet, not a measurement: for a promotion aimed at Rwandans, a variant may put the hook in Kinyarwanda first with the English line below ('Turi kuri Promotion / We are on promotion'), next to the number. Use it as one variant of a series, not the default; the voice still speaks English (voice-language).
short: A bet: one variant may put the hook in Kinyarwanda first, English below ('Turi kuri Promotion / We are on promotion'), beside the number.
why: Only 4 of 34 Kigali Instagram reels use Kinyarwanda, but the best of them (La Paix Technology, 161K plays on 751 followers) pairs a Kinyarwanda promotion line with the number on screen. Too few rows to call it a pattern; worth testing through our own results.

rule: A page post is not an ad: no price strip, no phone bar and no 'order now' line on screen by default. The offer, the price and the contact go in the caption; put an overlay on only when the owner marks the post as a promotion.
short: A post, not an ad: no price strip, no phone bar, no order line on screen; offer, price and contact in the caption.
why: Only 1 of 20 organic reels from 12 big Rwandan pages shows a price and a phone (Piramie, re-using an ad poster); the reels that reached furthest show a place or a moment (ONOMO's silent dining-room film 310K views, CANAL+'s Amavubi highlights 54K, RwandAir's staff moments 18K).

rule: Keep a post short and visual: 12 to 25 s in about 3 beats of 5 s, open on the most beautiful or most human frame (a real face, a pour, the venue at golden hour), and end on a clean logo card or the shop sign.
short: Posts: 12 to 25 s, 3 beats of about 5 s; open on the most beautiful or human frame, end on the logo or the shop sign.
why: The organic reels run a median 20 s (15 of 20 are 30 s or less) with about 3 cuts per 10 s, against 34 s for Rwandan ads; they open on a place, a face or the product, never on a price.

rule: Write a post caption of 10 to 25 words: one friendly line in the owner's language mix and 0 to 3 hashtags (the city and the brand only, keeping Kinyarwanda tags such as #amajyambere where they fit). Add the phone, the price and the place on a second line only for a real offer or an event.
short: Post caption: one friendly line of 10 to 25 words, 0 to 3 hashtags (city, brand); contact on a second line only for a real offer or event.
why: Organic captions are a median 13 words, 14 of 20 carry no hashtag, and only the offer and event posts give a way to order; the ads' spec-list caption with price, address and number does not appear on these pages.

rule: In posts, show people and moments over products: staff greetings, a customer-service week, an event recap, behind the scenes, a sponsored match, a walk through the shop. Remembrance days (Kwibuka) get a quiet, respectful message only, never an offer, a product or music with a beat.
short: Posts: people and moments over products (staff, an event recap, behind the scenes, a walk through the shop); Kwibuka only a quiet, respectful message.
why: Reach on the big pages came from brand, staff and national-calendar content (RwandAir's staff moments and expo recap, CANAL+'s national-team highlights, Bralirwa's Peace Marathon, Inyange's basketball camp); Skol's Kwibuka post is a solemn remembrance.

rule: Keep a post warm and local: the original sound or a calm library track under readable text (it must still work muted), and no hard sell.
short: Posts: original sound or a calm library track, readable muted; no hard sell.
why: 16 of 20 organic reels keep their original audio; the one organic post with a real offer (Java House's buy-one-get-one) got 163 views while the warm, local ones reached thousands.

rule: Keep the product real: start from the owner's real product photo or a real clip of it; the motion, the light, the background and the camera moves may be generated around it.
short: The product is always the owner's real photo or clip; only the motion, light and background around it may be generated.
why: No East African retailer was found using AI for its own advert; the AI business clips are AI studios' sales demos (generated boutiques, salons, a drink), which drew a median 5 comments. The one real-product-plus-motion example had 77 likes and 3 comments, so this is early evidence.

rule: Keep the shop, the place and the proof real: never generate a shop front, a school, a street or a home and present it as the business's own; use the owner's photo of the place and generate only what is around it.
short: Never generate the shop, the school or the street as the business's own; use the owner's photo of the place.
why: The only 'ni AI' (it's AI) comments seen were about places: a Chinese school posted as a Rwandan one ('this is not true, I study there') and a fashion clip that looked filmed at home, not in a shop. Generated villas and shops appear only in AI studios' demos.

rule: Prefer the owner's real face and voice for trust content (clinics, schools, services, testimonials); a generated presenter only for non-trust content, never as the owner or a customer; an AI voice only as a plain voice-over with burned-in captions.
short: Real face and voice for trust content; a generated presenter never as the owner or a customer; an AI voice only plain and captioned.
why: Generated people appear in 12 of the 20 AI-made clips, and the studios' demos with them drew a median 5 comments against 42 for real Rwandan shop clips. Whether an AI voice is accepted is unknown (one clip, 1 comment).

rule: Where the visuals are generated, add one short caption line ('AI-assisted visuals, real product') and keep the platform's own AI label; never say a generated scene is real.
short: Generated visuals: one caption line ('AI-assisted visuals, real product') and the platform's label; never call a generated scene real.
why: All five labelled AI entertainment clips still reached thousands of likes (32.7K for AI babies, 8.1K for a Kinyarwanda AI comedy), so a label did not stop reach there; how a disclosure changes a sales clip is untested.

rule: Never show income proof or payment screenshots: no MoMo, M-Money or bank SMS ('You have received 85000 RWF'), no piles of cash, no 'earn X a day' or 'get rich' lines.
short: No income proof: no fake M-Money or bank SMS, no cash piles, no 'get rich' lines.
why: Seen on TikTok and YouTube Shorts as MoMo screenshots next to a WhatsApp number: the pattern of scams. It destroys trust and breaks ad policy; the caption researcher skipped a dozen such chain posts.

rule: Never invent a price, a discount, a stock count ('only a few left'), an end date, a delivery promise, an award, a result or a number.
short: No invented price, discount, stock count, end date, delivery promise, award or result.
why: Owner rule for every engine; the ad must be true for the business that posts it.

rule: No 'best', 'cheapest', 'biggest' or 'most affordable in Kigali' unless the owner wrote it; then use their words exactly.
short: No 'best', 'cheapest', 'most affordable in Kigali' unless the owner wrote it.
why: Superlatives are common in the research (BEST BURGERS IN KIGALI, THE MOST CHEAPEST IPHONES) but only the business can stand behind them.

rule: No skin, body, weight or medical before/after and no health promises (tummy trimming, curing snoring, clearing acne).
short: No skin, body, weight or medical before/after, no health promises.
why: Seen in the research (split-face breakouts, body massager claims) but against Meta and TikTok policy and the owner's rules.

rule: No fake reviews, testimonials or comments: a fictional presenter never claims to be a real customer, and a 'Replying to' card only quotes a real question.
short: No fake reviews or comments; a fictional presenter never poses as a real customer.
why: UGC and comment-reply formats work because viewers believe them.

rule: No famous brands, logos or people that are not the business's own, and no lookalikes (the AI 'McDonald's' or 'Dior' style ads are not to be copied).
short: No famous brands, logos, people or lookalikes that are not the business's own.
why: Trademark and likeness rules; AI-creator showcase clips use them, client ads must not.

rule: Never leave another app's watermark or template tag in the video (TikTok logo, CapCut tag).
short: No other app's watermark or template tag.
why: Facebook ads that reuse TikTok clips show the TikTok watermark; it looks second-hand.

rule: Do not copy the AI-creator wrapper (the prompt first, 'How to make this', 'Comment PROMPT') into a client's ad.
short: No 'how I made this' / 'Comment PROMPT' wrapper in a client ad.
why: It sells the tool, not the product; it is engagement bait for creators.

rule: No vague or choose-your-own discounts ('Drop 40% or 60%'): one clear offer, on a named product, at a real price.
short: No vague discounts ('40% or 60%'): one clear offer at a real price.
why: BuPulse policy, not a research finding: a choose-your-own discount cannot be checked against the owner's facts (no-invented-facts), and a muted viewer cannot tell which deal applies. The one researched clip with such a line ('Drop 40% or 60%', a Ghanaian phone store, 67.8K likes) did well, so the research does not show that vague discounts lose.

rule: No film, TV, football or music-video clips and no copyrighted songs: only the business's own photos and footage, generated shots and the BuPulse music library.
short: No film, TV, football clips or copyrighted songs.
why: The For You feed is full of borrowed clips (football, films); an ad account gets them muted or taken down.

rule: No two-minute scrolling lists in an ad: at most about 5 items, one per beat, or one price card that stays up.
why: A 136 s word list kept likes low (2.3K); price lists that work fit in one frame.

rule: 'Start your business with us' only for real wholesalers, and never with an income promise ('make $10k', 'say goodbye to poverty').
short: 'Start your business with us' only for real wholesalers, never with income promises.
why: Business-idea clips sell hope; a client ad must sell stock at a price.

rule: Do not copy the polished brand-film look of hotels and big brands (no price, no number) for a small seller: their ads can afford to skip the contact, a small business cannot.
short: No polished brand film without a price and number for a small seller.
why: ONOMO and Dilara, with brand budgets, show no number in the video; small Rwandan sellers mostly do show one, though a florist's 3 s gift loop ran 228 days without it.

rule: Do not write or say 'subscribe', 'like and follow' or 'hit the bell' in a client's Short: the platform draws its own button and the ad must point to the business.
short: No 'subscribe' or 'like and follow' lines.
why: None of the 36 Shorts asks to subscribe; YouTube shows the button next to the channel.

rule: Do not answer a price question with 'Inbox' or 'Twandikire kuri WhatsApp' alone: the price belongs in the video and the caption, and a reply gives the price, the area or one clear route.
short: No bare 'Inbox' replies to price questions; the price is in the video and the caption.
why: One Kigali fashion hub gave the same WhatsApp redirect four times under price questions, and viewers answered 'Is the price a secret???'.
